solution:
Kameda and Umio were historical political rivals: Kameda was a king, and Umio was a duke. The comparison concerned their excavated skeletal remains, including photographs shown during a history lecture.
Their culture normally cremated the dead. Kameda’s fragmented bones were consistent with a proper cremation and an honourable royal burial.
Umio’s intact skeleton indicated that his body had instead been buried without cremation. The accepted historical explanation was that Kameda’s agents had poisoned Umio and secretly disposed of his body.
Consequently, Umio’s better-preserved remains suggested that he had lost the political struggle and been denied a proper funeral. They did not indicate that he had survived or defeated Kameda.
canonical_facts: Kameda the king and Umio the duke were political rivals, and the compared objects are excavated remains shown in a history lecture
Their culture normally cremates the dead
The king’s fragmented bones indicate normal cremation and an honorable burial
The duke’s intact skeleton indicates burial without cremation
The accepted account is that the king’s agents poisoned and secretly buried the duke
Better preservation therefore indicates the duke lost and was denied the customary funeral, not that he survived
explicit_negatives: An intact skeleton does not mean the duke survived or won.
They are remains being discussed, not living men fighting in the current scene.
unknown_details: The precise poison and excavation date are unspecified. Do not claim a photograph alone proves poisoning; it belongs to the accepted historical account.
irrelevant_details: Unspecified names, brands, colors and exact dates are incidental.

event_order: The king Kameda and duke Umio are political rivals.
The accepted historical account is that Kameda’s agents poison Umio and secretly bury his body without cremation.
Kameda receives the customary cremation and honorable burial. Do not infer an exact relative death date not supplied.
Later excavations reveal fragmented royal remains and an intact ducal skeleton; people compare photographs in a history lecture.
label_boundaries: No damage refers to the excavated skeleton, not Umio being alive and physically unharmed.
Political defeat and denial of a customary funeral are the relevant social loss.
The poisoning removes a political rival: a practical objective and intervention in the struggle, not an aimless exposure.
Poisoning does not establish a military chemical weapon, inhalation, or a named government agency. Resolve authority to the king’s agents when context supports it; do not invent a new institution.
